source: Bazazi, von Zimmermann, Bahrami, Richardson (2019) Self-serving incentives impair collective decisions by increasing conformity
finding: Seeing the group mean cut diversity and raised group error only when people were paid for their own accuracy. Under group-based pay, social information did little.
numbers: N=141 in 23 groups of 4-8 (70 individual pay, 71 collective pay); 16 London map questions; 2x2 within design (pay x social info). Diversity: social info effect MPE 95.85% overall, 99.88% under individual pay, 73.35% under collective pay. Group error: MPE 98.32% overall, 99.57% individual pay, 69.13% collective pay. Payoff main effect weak (diversity MPE 76.25%, error 65.35%).
quote: When rewarded for the accuracy of their individual responses, participants converged to the group mean
limits: Single lab, one task (spatial estimation), subject-pool participants, social info was only the group mean shown once between two answers. Bayesian MPE, not a classic p-value. Pay was a prize draw. Collective-pay null is 'little evidence', not shown equal.
agent_relevance: What drives a copy-the-group move is reward for own accuracy. Our scaffold should not reward each attempt for agreeing with others; keep attempts isolated (G4/G9) and judge the pooled result.

source: Bazazi et al. (2019) design detail: two-response paradigm and measures
finding: Design: Response 1 (private), then the mean of Response 1 shown as a star, then Response 2. Diversity was the distance of each final answer from the Response 1 mean; error was the distance of the final group mean from truth.
numbers: Each trial: 5 s map view, answer 1, 5 s second view with or without star, answer 2, then truth shown. Individual-pay feedback: told if dot was in the correct cell of a 3x4 grid. Collective-pay feedback: group mean shown on shared display. Four counterbalanced block orders.
limits: Showing only the mean removes spread information; the authors argue this gives the strongest conformity pull. Results may be weaker with raw individual answers.
agent_relevance: A copy-the-mean prompt (aggregate shown to each sampled attempt) is the strongest-pull format for an LLM too. If any cross-attempt sharing is used, share raw answers late, not a mean early.

source: Bazazi et al. (2019) discussion: where copying helps
finding: The authors note that copying can help in problem-solving tasks because the group reaches a good-enough answer fast. They note that pliability varies by person and by distance from the group.
numbers: Cites that people adjust more when their view is far from the group. No new numbers.
limits: This is the paper's own caveat, not a test. The effect depends on task type: estimation (diversity matters) versus search (convergence can help).
agent_relevance: Isolation helps estimation-like and sampling-based tasks. For search with a verifier, sharing partial results may be fine. Do not apply isolation blindly.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect
finding: Founding study. Subjects re-estimated five times; they saw nothing (control), the average, or all individual answers. Social influence shrank the spread of answers without lowering the collective error (social influence effect), pushed the truth to the edge of the answer range (range reduction), and raised confidence without better accuracy (confidence effect).
numbers: N=144 ETH Zurich students, 12 sessions of 12; 6 geography and crime-statistics questions; five consecutive estimates per question; real money stakes; each session had 2 questions per condition (control, aggregated, full information); confidence on a 6-point scale. Geometric mean was closer to truth than individuals in 77.1% of cases. Table 1 examples: Swiss population density true 184, arithmetic mean 2,644 (+1,337.2%), geometric mean 132 (-28.1%), median 130 (-29.3%); Swiss-Italian border true 734, geometric mean 338 (-54%).
quote: even mild social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect in simple estimation tasks
limits: Small sample, students, hard skewed numeric questions; the diversity-versus-error finding rests on the squared-error measure that Jayles 2017 shows is partly an identity. Text read from a copy of the PMC page on disk; tables beyond Table 1 not checked.
agent_relevance: Root evidence for isolating attempts: copying shrinks diversity without buying accuracy, and makes the group feel surer.

source: Jayles, Kim, Escobedo, Cezera, Blanchet, Kameda, Sire, Theraulaz (2017) How social information can improve estimation accuracy in human groups
finding: Strongest counter-evidence and a measurement critique. The Lorenz-style 'diversity falls, error unchanged' result is partly a measurement artifact: mean squared individual error = squared error of the mean + diversity, so falling diversity cannot hurt that measure. With controlled good information, social influence improves the group.
numbers: France: 29 hard questions, 5,394 x2 estimates; sequences of 20 humans plus virtual experts giving the truth at 0, 20, 43, 80% (n=0,5,15,80 added); social info = geometric mean of 1 or 3 prior answers. Median sensitivity S = 0.34. Japan replication gave near-identical S distribution. With rho=0% no significant gain in collective performance; gains grow with rho; adopters best for rho>=40%.
limits: Needs reliable information in the stream; at 0% experts no gain (agrees with Lorenz). Hard, low-demonstrability questions. Sequential local social information, not simultaneous.
agent_relevance: Quality of what is shared decides the outcome. Copying helps only when what is copied is more right than the copier. For an LLM, a verified partial result is shareable; an unverified peer answer is not.

source: Jayles et al. (2017) individual traits and the distance effect
finding: Sensitivity to influence rises with the gap between own estimate and the group, up to about 2.5 orders of magnitude. Confident people follow less and are more accurate before influence; but over-confident keepers lose value others hold.
numbers: Linear cusp relation of S vs D up to t about 2.5 orders of magnitude; only about 14% of data beyond 3 orders. Confident quarter: S=0 peak about 7 times the S=1 peak; followers: less than 2 times. Contradicting was the only category whose accuracy got worse with more expert information. Model predicts a modest overestimate fed to the group helps because humans underestimate.
limits: Categories formed from the first 24 questions, tested on questions 25-29. Model had no explicit confidence.
agent_relevance: Attempts far from the pack should not be pulled toward it automatically; a confidence-weighted, evidence-gated update is better than averaging.

source: Jayles, Sire, Kurvers (2021) Impact of sharing full versus averaged social information on social influence and estimation accuracy
finding: Showing all peer estimates versus only their average gave comparable accuracy gains, but people follow an average more than a list, and more so the larger the group behind the average.
numbers: 18 groups, 3 treatments (Sorted, Unsorted, Aggregated) x 6 values of tau (1,3,5,7,9,11) = 18 conditions; 42 questions x 12 subjects = 504 estimates per condition; between-subject treatment. Second estimates narrow after sharing. People follow social info more when it is above their own estimate than below.
limits: Groups of 12, estimation questions; accuracy gain comparable, not larger, for full info.
agent_relevance: Format of shared information changes how hard the pull is (an aggregate pulls harder). If one attempt sees others, show the spread, not just the mean.

source: Almaatouq, Rahimian, Burton, Alhajri (2022) The distribution of initial estimates moderates the effect of social influence on the wisdom of the crowd
finding: Reconciles conflicting results. Whether influence helps depends on the shape of the first estimates: if the crowd is centred near the truth, a few dominant voices hurt; if estimates are heavy-tailed or skewed, centralised influence can help.
numbers: Reanalysis of four published lab experiments: 2,885 participants, 99 independent groups, 54 estimation tasks, 15,562 individual and 687 collective estimates. Heavy-tailedness measured by R (log-normal vs normal fit). The interaction centralisation x R predicts when the group improves or degrades.
limits: Theory assumes a convex combination of initial estimates; centralisation is inferred, not measured, in most datasets.
agent_relevance: Explains why equal-weight pooling (G4) works for symmetric errors but a verified leader answer may beat it with skewed errors. Check error shape before choosing majority vs leader.

source: Madirolas & de Polavieja (2015) Improving collective estimations using resistance to social influence
finding: Humans combine private and social estimates as a weighted geometric mean. Selecting people who resist influence gives much better group estimates than the plain crowd; declared confidence did not help.
numbers: Reanalysis of Lorenz 2011 data (six Swiss questions). Example: resisting-subgroup error of -17% of true value 9272 versus -60% for the standard crowd (3685). Other resisting groups: -28%, -32%, -18% versus -60%. Simulated error reductions of -69%, -67%, -71%, -67% for different weight settings.
limits: Post-hoc reanalysis of one dataset; needs a before and after answer per person.
agent_relevance: A cheap signal: attempts that do not move when shown peers carry independent information. For an LLM, stability under peer exposure could be a weak confidence signal. Untested.

source: Madirolas & de Polavieja (2015) on why shared answers amplify bias
finding: After influence the group is more peaked around a possibly wrong value, giving a false sense of agreement.
numbers: Notes Galton's 784 farmers: the median beat single estimates.
limits: Mechanism claim from a model, consistent with Lorenz.
agent_relevance: Agreement among attempts that saw each other is not evidence of correctness (G9).

source: Wang, Su, Wang, Plotkin (2025) Individual incentives that promote collective intelligence
finding: Imitating successful peers reduces diversity and inhibits collective intelligence. Two payoff schemes keep diversity: reward experts, or reward reformers whose input reduces collective error even if personally wrong. The reformer reward is more robust.
numbers: Task: outcome depends linearly on many random factors; each agent sees one factor; the collective prediction is the average. Both schemes provably maintain diversity. Rewards based on collective error were more robust across problem settings than rewards on personal accuracy.
limits: Theory and simulation, not human data; assumes independent factors and a linear outcome.
agent_relevance: Matches Bazazi's collective-pay result. When selecting or training agents, reward marginal contribution to the ensemble, not own accuracy.

source: Stein, Cruz, Grossi, Testori (2026) Free information disrupts even Bayesian crowds
finding: Even perfect, cooperative Bayesian agents get less accurate when they swap unlimited evidence in homophilous encounters. Limiting how much is exchanged can help.
numbers: Agent-based model, N=100 agents. Beliefs converge on truth only when communication capacity is high AND homophily is low. Robust to 1<|S|<10 initial signals per agent.
limits: Computational thought experiment, no human or LLM data; the authors say so.
agent_relevance: Clones of one model are maximal homophily. Do not assume more sharing between attempts helps; cap what passes between them.

source: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2026) Collective problem decomposition improves the wisdom of deliberative crowds
finding: Rival route to group accuracy: groups that split an estimate into parts and estimate the parts beat groups told to combine their first guesses.
numbers: 1,140 online text-chat deliberations over 3 studies. Study 1 N=500: spontaneous decomposition predicts lower error. Study 2 N=240: decomposition-instructed groups beat groups told to combine initial guesses. Study 3 N=160: benefit larger when applied collectively than individually.
limits: Structured deliberation, not mere exposure to a mean; chat text; estimation tasks.
agent_relevance: Fermi-style decomposition is a better thing to share than answers. Share intermediate quantities, not final values.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd of 925 forecasters. Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved them, but plain averaging of human and machine was better still.
numbers: Study 1: 12 LLMs, 31 binary questions, 3-month tournament, 925 human forecasters; LLM crowd statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd and better than a no-information benchmark. Study 2: exposure to the human median raised accuracy by 17 to 28% for GPT-4 and Claude 2; each question posed 3 times pre and post (6 forecasts per model per question); simple averaging beat updating.
limits: 2023-era models, one tournament, binary questions. The exposed LLM saw a median once.
agent_relevance: Independent attempts pooled equal the crowd; updating on a shown crowd gives less than just pooling. Supports aggregate-after, not share-then-update.

source: Kraidia et al. (2026) When collaboration fails: persuasion-driven adversarial influence in multi-agent LLMs
finding: One confident adversarial agent in an LLM debate can drag the group. Adding agents or debate rounds does not fix it; Best-of-N and RAG make the attack more persuasive.
numbers: Accuracy down 10-40%; agreement on wrong answers up by more than 30%. Datasets: MMLU, TruthfulQA, MedMCQA, SCALR, Math, Chess. Models include GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-Turbo, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Yi. GPT-3.5 lost up to 30% accuracy; agreement with the adversary often over 0.40. Simple prompt warnings were not enough.
limits: The adversary is designed and given a target claim; shows vulnerability, not a natural base rate.
agent_relevance: A pooled-debate scaffold is open to one confident bad voice. Isolation plus verification beats debate (G4, G9).

source: Coppolillo, Manco, Aiello (2026) Unmasking conversational bias in AI multiagent systems
finding: Pairs of LLMs given the same stance drifted away from it when talking, especially conservative pairs, though like-minded agents should not move.
numbers: Echo-chamber test with models including GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, Nous-Hermes-2-Mixtral, Gemma. Significant stance shifts found; questionnaire bias detectors did not see it.
limits: Opinion topics, not factual estimates; pairs only.
agent_relevance: Models drift toward their own prior when talking, so conversation adds a systematic bias, not just noise.

source: Ueshima, Jones, Christakis (2024) Simple autonomous agents can enhance creative semantic discovery by human groups
finding: Bots that pass on the most similar noun helped groups when the landscape was easy to navigate, not otherwise.
numbers: N=1875 participants in 125 networks of 15 nodes, sometimes plus 2 bots; 20,000-noun semantic space (word2vec 300-d); three bot strategies (random, most similar, least similar). Groups beat isolated individuals.
limits: Search task with graded payoff, not factual estimation; effect depends on difficulty.
agent_relevance: Sharing helps in smooth search landscapes and can hurt in rugged ones. Task type is the moderator.

source: Denton, Feldman, Johannemann (2026) Conformity to popular, not average, opinions
finding: People copy clusters, not averages. A cluster-copy model fits human data better than averaging models under many conditions and can lower average accuracy.
numbers: Fit to human decision data and evolutionary simulations on static and adaptive networks; the conformity model can shift populations faster toward extreme opinions.
limits: Model comparison on existing data; better fit in many but not all conditions.
agent_relevance: If peers split into two camps, copiers pick one camp, not the middle. Treat a majority of mutually exposed attempts as one camp, not independent votes.

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds
finding: From memory: in decentralised networks social influence improved accuracy; in centralised networks it hurt. Not read this session.
numbers: Unverified: about 1,360 subjects, networks of 40, estimation questions.
limits: Not opened; unverified. Almaatouq 2022 (opened) cites the centralisation result and says it depends on the shape of initial estimates.
agent_relevance: Equal voice across attempts beats a dominant voice when errors are symmetric.

source: Becker, Porter, Centola (2019) The wisdom of partisan crowds
finding: From memory: partisan groups in decentralised networks became more accurate and less biased on politically charged facts after interaction. Not read.
numbers: Unverified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Even biased agents can gain from equal-voice interaction on shared factual evidence; so isolation is not universally best.

source: Mann & Helbing (2017) Optimal incentives for collective intelligence
finding: From memory: an incentive rewarding accuracy plus minority-opinion correctness can keep diversity. Bazazi 2019 (opened) cites it as theory that predicted individual pay yields good diversity; Bazazi's data contradicted the naive reading.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Incentive design matters; any reward we use for ensembles should include a diversity or marginal-contribution term.

source: Frey & van de Rijt (2021) Social influence undermines the wisdom of the crowd in sequential decision making
finding: From memory: in a sequential online experiment, influence on later decision makers produced herding and worse crowd accuracy. Not read.
numbers: Unverified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Sequential exposure (later attempts see earlier ones) is the risky ordering.

source: Gurcay, Mellers, Baron (2015) The power of social influence on estimation accuracy
finding: From memory: showing others' estimates improved individual accuracy in some conditions, more with larger groups. Not read.
numbers: Unverified.
limits: Not opened. Individual accuracy gains do not mean better pooled accuracy.
agent_relevance: Per-attempt accuracy can rise through copying while pooled accuracy does not; always score the pool.

source: Navajas, Niella, Garbulsky, Bahrami, Sigman (2018) Aggregated knowledge from a small number of debates outperforms the wisdom of large crowds
finding: From memory: averaging after small-group discussion beat averaging many independent guesses. Not read.
numbers: Unverified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Rival to isolation: short structured discussion in small groups, then pool. Fits Barrera 2026 (opened).

source: Page (2007) The Difference: diversity prediction theorem
finding: From memory: collective squared error = average individual squared error minus diversity. The identity behind the Jayles 2017 critique.
numbers: Identity G' = G + GD is stated in Jayles 2017 (opened); no figures from Page.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Diversity helps only when individual error is held fixed; copying lowers both.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: From memory: several model instances debating over rounds beat a single instance on reasoning and factual tasks. Not read.
numbers: Unverified.
limits: Not opened. Counterweight to Kraidia 2026 (opened).
agent_relevance: Debate can help when all agents are honest; harmful with one confident wrong agent. Needs a verifier.
